1:
Gill and Clarke both read the chapter as the plain answer to the complaint of the one before it, the prophet ordered to repeat in clearer terms what he first delivered in figure. Henry makes the same point a rule for preaching, that one who speaks with tongues should pray that he may interpret, and that when we speak to people about their souls we should study plainness, all men being left inexcusable and every mouth stopped. Ellicott ties the three commands, to set the face, to drop the word and to prophesy, back to the close of the preceding chapter, where what stands here as Jerusalem, the holy places and the land of Israel stood in figure.

Henry works the new oracle as a point-by-point translation of the old. The holy places were dignified above others, but being polluted, the word that used to drop in them now drops against them, and Zion is justly battered with her own artillery. The fire of the parable becomes the sword, and it is the sword of God, lying quiet in its sheath until he draws it. Where the fire devoured green tree and dry, the sword cuts off righteous and wicked alike. Henry will not let this collapse the difference: the graces and comforts of God make a great distinction where his providence seems to make none, and it is only in outward appearance that one event befalls both. The point is rather the greatness of the divine displeasure, that his eye spares not even the righteous, whose loss his mercy will make up some other way. He instances Daniel and his fellows, and Ezekiel himself, carried to Babylon at the beginning of the troubles, as a threatening omen to the land.

Clarke reaches the same ground by another road. He distinguishes the ways of being cut off, by the sword, by pestilence, by famine and by captivity, and observes that among the last two the righteous must have suffered with the wicked when there was no bread in the besieged city; yet their perishing was no loss to them, since no man ever complained of getting to heaven too soon. And had none but the wicked been carried away their case would have been hopeless, with none left to set a good example, preach repentance or reprove sin. Wesley states the principle in a line, that it is no unusual thing for the righteous to be involved with others in public calamities.

On the sword not returning, Clarke and Ellicott agree that its limit is the completion of its work, not any term of years. Ellicott sets it against earlier judgments arrested in mercy, the sword returned to the scabbard while its work was still incomplete, whereas this one will go on to the end; Clarke observes that it did not return till the king of Babylon had subdued every land from the Euphrates to the Nile. Wesley says only that it will not go back into the scabbard till it has done full execution.

The sign asked of the prophet is a sigh. Gill takes the breaking of the loins as a posture, the hands laid on them as of a woman in travail and held until the girdle breaks, so that the gesture shows the state of the people; Clarke and Wesley read it the same way. Ellicott grounds it in the loins as the seat of strength, whose breaking expresses entire prostration, and notes that it was done before their eyes, to provoke the question the next verse answers. Henry adds that the prophet must sigh though it made his own breast sore and though the profane would ridicule him for it, since ministers who would affect others must show themselves affected first; and that what was coming was no bugbear, but a thing that would melt every heart and leave every knee weak as water.
8:
Gill notes that some read this as a new prophecy of another sword, the Roman rather than the Chaldean, but takes it as an enlargement of what went before. Henry describes the weapon in stages. It is sharpened, that it may wound and make a sore slaughter, the wrath of God putting an edge on it and filling whatever instruments he uses with courage according to the service they are employed in. It is furbished, that it may glitter to the terror of those against whom it is drawn; if it has rusted in the scabbard for want of use it shall be rubbed bright, for though the glory of divine justice seems eclipsed during the delay of judgment, it will shine out again. Wesley glosses the furbishing in three words, made clean and bright, and Clarke traces the term to the French for polishing.

The hardest clause here is the one about the rod of the son, and Ellicott is frankest about it: the original is obscure in its extreme brevity, the versions and many commentators have changed the text without improvement, and the phrase may be taken as object or as subject. His own preference makes the clause an objection in the mouth of the hearer, that the rod of the son despises every tree, the promise to Judah being sure and his sceptre bound to remain whatever power rises against it. The objection was in a sense true, he allows, but those who raised it imagined it gave the kingdom a temporal security whatever its sins, and the prophet does not answer it except by going on with his prediction. Clarke reads the clause the other way, as the sword despising the power of the people God called his son, and asks whether the rod of Israel can be spared when the trees of Egypt and Assyria are cut down. Henry grants that the government of that people was a strong rod and the rod of his son, and that the sword makes nothing of it.

The prophet is then to cry and howl and smite upon the thigh. Gill marks the rise from sighing to crying and then to howling, the prophet acting the part to affect the people beforehand. Clarke takes the smiting of the thigh for a known gesture of grief and quotes a passage of Homer in which a god smites his thighs and cries out, giving it in the version of Cowper. Ellicott supplies the connection: you think the promise to Judah secures you, but do not deceive yourselves, and prepare for sorrow. Wesley calls the sign a token of the prophet sense of what they must suffer. Henry presses the repetition, that the sword of the heathen should be upon the people of God and upon all the princes of Israel, whose dignity was no more a security than their profession of religion.

The word about the trial closes the group and puzzles everyone. Ellicott reports great variety of interpretation and says neither text nor margin of the English is intelligible; the rendering he prefers is that the sword has already been proved on others, and asks what if this contemning sceptre shall be no more. Clarke reads it as a trial of strength between the Chaldeans and the Jews and of faith and patience in the righteous, and takes the contemning as the overthrow of the king, after which the regal government of Judea would be no more. Wesley states the condition plainly, that if king and kingdom despise this trial both shall be destroyed. Henry hears in it the fear of the godly that the sword will contemn even the rod, forgetting its commission to correct and becoming a sword indeed, like the axe that boasts against the one who hews with it; and he answers by insisting that it is a trial and no more than a trial.
14:
Gill takes the smiting of the hands as the clapping of one in an agony, or as encouragement to the enemy to use the sword he has drawn; Wesley reads it for amazement and sorrow, Ellicott simply as a gesture of strong emotion. On the sword doubled the third time Ellicott says the translation is obscure but the meaning plain, that the activity of the sword is intensified to the utmost. Clarke prefers a count: the king of Babylon came against Judea three times, against Jehoiakim, against Jeconiah and against Zedekiah, so that the sword had already been doubled and was now to come the third time. He also presses the word rendered slain, which he takes for soldier, so that the phrase is the sword of the soldiers and then of that great soldier, the conquering king. Ellicott takes the same word differently, as the overthrown rather than the killed, since it is used in a moral as well as a physical sense and elsewhere rendered polluted.

The word rendered the point of the sword occurs nowhere else, and Gill lists the guesses of the older authorities, the fear of the sword, or its cry, or the cry of the slain. Ellicott holds that the exact meaning is the glance or the whirl of the sword, whose whirling motion was to be everywhere, against all their gates; and he renders the multiplied ruins literally as multiplied stumbling blocks, trouble being on every side in the coming desolation and occasions for ill-advised action arising all around. On the sword being wrapped up, Clarke says it is not blunt but carefully sharpened and preserved for the slaughter, and Wesley that it was kept in the scabbard lest it be blunted; Ellicott prefers drawn, drawn out for the slaughter. Wesley extends the gates to those of cities, of palaces and of private houses.

The sword is then addressed directly. Ellicott complains that the animation of the address is lost in the English, the sword being spoken to as a host and told to close ranks right and set itself left, ready for action in every quarter. Gill takes the command as an order to unite with other swords and spare none as it goes, and Clarke as a promise of success whichever way it turns, against Ammon or Judea or Egypt. When the divine hands are smitten together in turn, Wesley calls it a token of approbation, Gill hesitates between concern and indignation, and Ellicott explains the fury coming to rest as its having accomplished its purpose and having nothing more to do.

Ellicott marks the eighteenth verse as the opening of the third and final prophecy of the chapter, more explicit than the others and carrying a new subject, since the desolation is now said to be effected by the king of Babylon, whose conquests will extend to the Ammonites. Henry says the prophet must draw two roads as on a map and bring the army to the place where they part, both coming out of one land; there the king pauses, resolved on the ruin of both but undetermined which to attack first, so that his politics leave him at a loss. Ellicott insists the whole is a vision rather than a piece of open interference, since the roads from Babylon to Rabbath and to Jerusalem run together for many hundred miles and the prophet cannot have stood at their parting. He also corrects the rendering choose thou a place: the verb never means choose nor the noun place, and the sense is to make a hand, that is, a finger-post set up to direct the king on his march. Wesley has the prophet paint the roads on a tile and set the army at the desert edge. Clarke asks why the Ammonites should be threatened, and answers that they had been united with Zedekiah against the Chaldeans.
21:
Gill has the prophet describe as already done what he foresees, the king halting where the road from Babylon divides, to Jerusalem on the right and to Rabbath on the left, meaning to take both but unsettled which first. Clarke sets out the three kinds of divination used, by arrows, by images and by entrails, and describes the arrow rite as still practised among the Arabs: three headless arrows, one marked to command, one to forbid and one blank, drawn from a bag, the blank requiring a fresh draw. Ellicott prefers shook his arrows to made his arrows bright, notes the practice in Mesopotamia and among the Greeks, one instance of it in Homer, and that it lasted among the Arabs until the Koran forbade it. On the images Ellicott says nothing is known of their use, while Wesley supposes the devil answered from them by permission; on the liver, Ellicott points to a custom familiar from classical literature and attested in Babylonia, while Clarke thinks the inspection served only to show whether the victim was sound, a diseased animal being a bad omen.

The lot falls to the right. Gill says what looked to the king like divination was overruled by providence to send him where he was designed to go, and Clarke supposes two arrows written, one Jerusalem and one Riblath, with a third blank. Ellicott corrects at his right hand to into his right hand came the divination that determined his course, and would read captains as battering rams. The Jews, says Gill, laughed at the whole thing as a heathenish practice from which nothing would come. Ellicott grants they were determined not to believe it, but suspects mixed with that a secret consciousness of the worthlessness of the idolatries they practised themselves. On those that have sworn oaths, Clarke and Wesley name Zedekiah and his princes, bound by oath to the king of Babylon and expecting Egyptian help; Ellicott adds that they knew their own violation of those oaths and yet persuaded themselves their intrigues were unknown, and refers the remembering of the iniquity to the king rather than to God.

Gill takes the profanity of the prince for his violated oath and adds that though ordinary persons may not call a king wicked, a prophet with a commission from God may. Clarke gives the same two grounds, the broken oath and opposition to the prophet. Ellicott observes that the word rendered profane is the one rendered slain earlier and would put overthrown in both places, what is close at hand being described as accomplished; and he explains the time of the iniquity of the end as that final transgression closed by the immediate manifestation of judgment, iniquity being allowed its course through forbearance and arrested at its height.

Ellicott makes the strongest claim on the last two verses. The word rendered diadem is elsewhere always the mitre of the high priest, so that the priestly office fell with the royal, and neither was recovered in full power after the captivity; the four verbs are infinitives, better rendered as passives, the mitre shall be removed and the crown taken off, the low exalted and the high abased; and this not this means an utter change of the whole existing state. Wesley identifies the one exalted as Jeconiah, advanced in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, while Clarke makes him Gedaliah. Gill takes the threefold overturning for the utter abolition of the kingly power rather than, as one authority held, for three generations, and reads it as covering the troubled interval to the coming of the Messiah; Clarke reports a reading of the three as the conquests under Jehoiakim, Jeconiah and Zedekiah. Ellicott and Wesley both take the coming one as the promised heir in whom the priestly and royal prerogatives are united, everything being thrown until then into a condition of flux without settlement.
28:
Gill takes the closing oracle as an enlargement of the earlier one, the second of the two roads now being followed to its end. Ellicott explains why it was needed: the king having turned aside to Jerusalem, the inference would be that the Ammonites might escape altogether, and the heathen would draw from the ruin of the people of God beside the immunity of their old enemies conclusions unworthy of his power; so this is added to show that judgment falls on them too, and without the promise given to Israel. Clarke and Ellicott date the fulfilment a few years after the taking of Jerusalem, Ellicott adding that the Ammonites dwindled until their name and place among the nations disappeared.

Henry reads the reproach as twofold. There is the reproach the Ammonites brought on themselves by hearkening to their own false prophets, who promised them perpetual safety while the countries around were laid waste; those who feed on self-conceit in prosperity, he says, prepare matter for self-reproach in calamity. And there is the reproach they cast on the people of God, triumphing in their afflictions and so adding to them, which he calls barbarous and inhuman; those are ripening apace for misery who trample on the people of God in distress, when they ought rather to tremble at judgment beginning at his house. Gill and Ellicott both note that the Ammonites had their own seers and diviners, and Wesley calls them astrologers and soothsayers who deceived them with fair but false divinations.

The image of the fall is exact. Ellicott explains that Judah is to fall first and Ammon immediately after, as it were upon the necks of those already slain, the figure taken from a battle in which one warrior falls on the body of the man who fell before him; Wesley reads it the same way, of one stumbling among a multitude of slain. On the end of their iniquity Ellicott is careful that it comes not through repentance but because iniquity ceases of necessity with the sinner death. Where the English asks whether the sword shall return to its sheath, Ellicott finds nothing in the original to mark a question or the first person, and takes it as a command to the Ammonites, return it into the sheath, meaning all resistance will be vain. Gill keeps the question and answers it, that the sword shall not be put up until they are consumed, and Henry that it does not return until God causes it to, he being in one mind, and who can turn him?

Ellicott notes that the figure of the sword, held through the whole chapter, is dropped at the end and replaced by fire, the consuming fire of divine wrath blown against Ammon as fire is turned by the wind upon a forest. Henry draws the same image out, that the least drop of that indignation creates anguish enough for the soul that does evil, and that wicked men make themselves fuel to the fire which consumes them. On the brutish men skilful to destroy, Henry gives the sharpest description in the chapter, men with the wit of men to do the work of wild beasts, whose reason makes them skilful but who have no compassion, so that they are skilful only to destroy; and yet they serve a purpose, the Ammonites being justly given into such hands because they themselves delighted in destruction. Henry presses the place of judgment too, that they are judged where they were created and seemed to have taken root, and closes on the irreparable ruin, their name justly blotted out who would have had the name of Israel for ever lost. Clarke refers the judging instead to the madness that came on the king of Babylon after his return, and Ellicott and Gill agree that for Ammon there is no future such as was promised to Israel.
